fields.title: Introducing aimbaza.org — the new MbazaNLP community hub
fields.excerpt: MbazaNLP has a new home. aimbaza.org brings together our models, datasets, events, and community resources in one place — built on Django and open-source from day one.
fields.body:
MbazaNLP has been building open-source NLP tools for Kinyarwanda and East African languages since its founding. Until now, our community presence has been spread across GitHub, HuggingFace, and a static website that was difficult to keep up to date.

Today we are launching aimbaza.org — a new community hub built on Django that brings everything together.

What's on the site

Projects & Models lists all 13 of our publicly available models across machine translation, speech recognition, text-to-speech, and conversational AI — all freely available on HuggingFace under open licences.

Opportunities surfaces grants, fellowships, and computing access (including DFKI HPC) relevant to African language NLP researchers.

Events will track past and upcoming workshops, sprints, and community calls.

The Gallery captures photos from our community events, starting with the Bakame Hackathon in April 2023.

Contribute explains how to get involved — whether through data, code, documentation, or community support.

Services & Offerings documents what MbazaNLP can offer to research partners and organisations looking to work with us.

Open infrastructure

The site is open-source and deployed from the MBAZA-NLP/aimbaza.org repository on GitHub. The CI/CD pipeline runs Black, Flake8, and automated tests on every pull request. We welcome contributions to the site itself — see the Contribute page for the pull request workflow.

What's next

In the coming weeks we will be adding a community blog with release notes for our models, technical posts from community members, and an events calendar. We are also building a Slack news bot that will post weekly digests of upcoming events and opportunities directly to our community workspace.

Join us on Slack at aimbaza.slack.com or browse the models at huggingface.co/mbazaNLP.

fields.title: Model documentation sprint: 13 HuggingFace improvements submitted
fields.excerpt: As part of the GIZ-funded community maintenance work, we submitted 13 pull requests across all MbazaNLP HuggingFace models and datasets, addressing every critical documentation gap found in the community audit.
fields.body:
As part of the GIZ-funded community maintenance contract, the first major work package was a systematic documentation audit and improvement sprint across all MbazaNLP models on HuggingFace.

The audit found that no model had a complete model card. Only 1 of 11 models had an Intended Use section. Several models had blank README files, and two had no card at all. We submitted 13 pull requests on 21 May 2026 covering every model and dataset in the mbazaNLP organisation.

What we fixed

Intended Use sections were added to all 10 models that were missing them. A clear statement of what a model is for — and what it should not be used for — is the most basic documentation requirement for responsible AI publishing.

Limitations and Bias & Fairness sections were added across all 13 models. Responsible disclosure of model limitations is a requirement under the HuggingFace Model Card specification.

BibTeX citation blocks were added to all 13 models. This makes it possible for researchers to cite MbazaNLP models in academic papers, which is important for the community's visibility and recognition in the research literature.

Code loading examples were added to three models that had none: bakame-chatbot-kinyarwanda, kinyarwanda-tts-model, and kinyarwanda-coqui-stt-model. A model with no usage example is effectively inaccessible to practitioners who want to experiment with it.

Translation model code examples were updated for compatibility with Transformers v5. The previous examples used the v4 API, which fails for users installing the latest version of the library.

License conflicts were resolved in kinyarwanda-coqui-stt-model, where the declared licence was inconsistent with the intended apache-2.0 release.

Numeric evaluation results were added to three quantized models that had no performance figures. A model card without metrics gives users no basis for comparing or selecting models.

Language tags were added to NLLB-Education, enabling the HuggingFace search system to surface the model to Kinyarwanda researchers.

Dataset improvements

PIQA-kin (a Kinyarwanda adaptation of the Physical Intuition Question Answering benchmark) received its first complete dataset card. The dataset had 100 downloads and 15 likes but no documentation. The new card describes the task, the data format, the collection process, and appropriate use cases.

NMT_Education_parallel_data_en_kin had a schema mismatch in its test split that was causing the HuggingFace dataset viewer to fail. The fix adds a configs/dataset_info YAML block with the correct column types, restoring the viewer for all users.

What's next

All 13 pull requests are open and awaiting merge by the respective model owners. If you own one of the mbazaNLP models, please review and merge your open PR — the links are in the community Slack #general channel.

In the next phase we will be publishing a standard model card template as a community resource on HuggingFace, so that all future MbazaNLP releases start from a complete, correctly formatted card rather than a blank README.

fields.title: Community update: aimbaza.org is live, engineering standards incoming, and a sprint in June
fields.excerpt: The new aimbaza.org site is now fully built and deployed to staging. Engineering standards are ready for publication. And we are running a community sprint on 14–15 June — open to all skill levels.
fields.body:
This is the second community release note from the GIZ-funded MbazaNLP maintenance work. It covers what has shipped since the model documentation sprint in May, what is coming next, and how to get involved.

aimbaza.org is feature-complete on staging

The replacement community website is now fully built and deployed to https://robo-advisor-4fl4.onrender.com. All nine planned pages are live:

Home and About carry over the community mission and partner acknowledgements. Projects & Models lists all 13 HuggingFace models and datasets with direct links. Community links out to Slack, GitHub, HuggingFace, and email. Events shows the community calendar plus a curated list of international AI and NLP events with sponsorship opportunities highlighted. Blog is where you are reading this. Opportunities lists computing access (Google TPU Research Cloud, AWS Research Credits), grants (Lacuna Fund, Mozilla Technology Fund, AI4D Africa, GIZ Digital Transformation), and fellowships (Masakhane, Google for Startups Africa). Contribute explains how to get involved with code, data, documentation, or community support. Services & Offerings describes what MbazaNLP can offer to research partners. Gallery shows photos from the Bakame Community Hackathon (April 2023).

The site is open-source at github.com/ronn13/aimbaza.org and will transfer to the MBAZA-NLP organisation once org admin access is confirmed. Production deployment to aimbaza.org is scheduled to follow immediately after that transfer.

Engineering standards

A Community Engineering Standards repository has been scaffolded covering Python style (Black, Flake8, PEP 8), git workflow (branch naming, commit conventions, PR process), model and dataset card requirements, repository naming conventions, and CI workflow templates. The repository is ready to publish to MBAZA-NLP/engineering-standards once the org admin creates the repo.

A model card template is also ready for publication to HuggingFace as mbazaNLP/model-card-template. This will ensure all future model releases start from a complete, correctly formatted card.

HuggingFace model card PRs — action still needed

The 13 pull requests submitted on 21 May are still open. If you are a model owner, your PR is waiting for your review. The list of open PRs and their URLs is in the first release note on this blog. Merging these PRs is the single highest-impact action any model owner can take right now — the documentation gaps are visible to every visitor who finds the models through HuggingFace search.

Join us: community sprint, 14–15 June 2026

We are running a two-day community sprint in Kigali on Saturday and Sunday, 14–15 June 2026. The sprint is open to all skill levels — NLP researchers, developers, translators, and anyone curious about Kinyarwanda language technology.

Planned activities include model evaluation sessions (testing the translation, ASR, and TTS models against real-world use cases), a data contribution track for adding parallel sentences to the NMT dataset, a documentation track for reviewing and improving model cards after the PRs merge, and an onboarding session for new contributors.

Details and sign-up will be posted in the #events channel on Slack. Join us at aimbaza.slack.com.

What's next

The remaining priorities for June are: production deployment of aimbaza.org once the repo transfer unblocks, publication of the engineering standards repository, the June sprint, and the final monthly progress report and handover documentation due 30 June 2026.

fields.title: What MbazaNLP has built: a guide to our open Kinyarwanda AI models
fields.excerpt: MbazaNLP has published 13 open-source AI models for Kinyarwanda and East African languages. This post maps the full landscape — what each model does, how to load it, and where it fits in an NLP pipeline.
fields.body:
MbazaNLP has been quietly building open-source AI infrastructure for Kinyarwanda and East African languages for several years. The result is 13 publicly available models on HuggingFace, spanning machine translation, speech recognition, text-to-speech, and conversational AI. This post provides a practical guide to what exists and how to use it.

All models are available at huggingface.co/mbazaNLP and are licensed under Apache 2.0 or compatible open licences unless stated otherwise.

Machine Translation

MbazaNLP has the largest set of open English-Kinyarwanda translation models of any public organisation. All are fine-tuned on Meta's NLLB-200 (No Language Left Behind) base model.

Nllb_finetuned_general_en_kin is the general-domain translation model, suitable for most use cases. Nllb_finetuned_education_en_kin and Nllb_finetuned_tourism_en_kin are domain-adapted versions that perform better on educational and tourism content respectively — a useful reminder that domain matters significantly for low-resource MT.

For deployment on constrained hardware, Quantized_Nllb_Finetuned_Edu_En_Kin_8bit and Quantized_Nllb_Finetuned_Tourism_En_Kin_8bit are 8-bit quantized versions of the education and tourism models, reducing memory requirements by roughly half with modest quality trade-offs.

NLLB-Education is a larger model providing higher-quality translation for the education domain, intended for production deployments where hardware is less constrained.

To load any translation model:

from transformers import pipeline
translator = pipeline('translation', model='mbazaNLP/Nllb_finetuned_general_en_kin')
result = translator('Hello, how are you?', src_lang='eng_Latn', tgt_lang='kin_Latn')
print(result[0]['translation_text'])

Speech Recognition (ASR)

Three ASR models cover Kinyarwanda with different architectures and trade-offs.

Whisper-Small-Kinyarwanda is a fine-tuned version of OpenAI's Whisper Small model. Note: the model was fine-tuned using language='sw' (Swahili) as the Whisper language tag — Kinyarwanda does not have its own tag in the base Whisper model. This is documented in the model card.

Kinyarwanda_nemo_stt_conformer_model uses NVIDIA's NeMo Conformer-CTC architecture, which tends to perform well on clean speech. stt_rw_sw_lg_conformer_ctc_large extends coverage to a multilingual model supporting Kinyarwanda, Swahili, and Luganda in a single checkpoint.

kinyarwanda-coqui-stt-model uses Coqui STT (formerly Mozilla DeepSpeech). This was one of the earlier MbazaNLP models and demonstrates the community's work before the transition to Transformer-based architectures.

Text-to-Speech

kinyarwanda-tts-model provides Kinyarwanda speech synthesis. TTS for low-resource languages is significantly harder than ASR due to the need for high-quality single-speaker recordings, and this model represents a substantial data collection effort by the community.

Conversational AI

bakame-chatbot-kinyarwanda is the most-downloaded model in the MbazaNLP organisation. It powers the Bakame chatbot, a Kinyarwanda-language conversational AI that was the focus of the April 2023 Bakame Hackathon. The hackathon gathered community contributors to evaluate, extend, and improve the chatbot across a range of use cases.

Using the models

All models can be loaded with the HuggingFace Transformers library. The model cards on HuggingFace now include updated code examples following the recent documentation sprint. If you encounter any issues, open an issue on the relevant GitHub repository or post in the #models channel on our Slack workspace at aimbaza.slack.com.

Contributing

All models are open for improvement. If you have domain-specific data, evaluation benchmarks, or compute resources to contribute, we would like to hear from you. See the Contribute page on this site or reach out on Slack.
